title: Sign Conventions and Solved Numericals
notes: Sign Conventions for Spherical Mirrors
Standard Cartesian Convention
Think of the mirror as the center of a math graph. Left is negative, Right is positive. Up is positive, Down is negative.
Real images are always on the left and upside down → v is negative, m is negative.
Virtual images are always on the right and upright → v is positive, m is positive.
What Does "Real is Positive" (RIP) Mean?
Some textbooks use an alternative, non-Cartesian system called the "Real-is-Positive" (RIP) sign convention.
Distance rule: Distances to real things (real object, real focus, real image) are given a plus (+) sign.
Virtual rule: Distances to virtual things (virtual focus, virtual image) are given a minus (−) sign.
The catch: This rule applies strictly to distances (u, v, f), not to the magnification's orientation meaning. Even under RIP, a real image is still physically upside down.

Rule: In the RIP system, −m means a Virtual, Erect image. +m means a Real, Inverted image.
Magnification Formula Differs Between Systems
Standard Convention: m = −v/u
Real-is-Positive (RIP) System: m = v/u (the minus sign is dropped from the formula)
How the Sign of m is Determined in RIP
Because the formula is m = v/u, the sign of m depends entirely on whether the image is real or virtual:
Real Image: object distance (u) is real (+), image distance (v) is real (+). Therefore, m = +v/+u = Positive (+m).
Virtual Image: object distance (u) is real (+), image distance (v) is virtual (−). Therefore, m = −v/+u = Negative (−m).
The Core Point of Confusion
The confusion happens because the same physical image is described with completely opposite math signs depending on which system you choose.
Let's look at a Real, Inverted Image formed by a concave mirror: in the real world, the image is physically upside down and in front of the mirror.

How to Solve Problems Without Confusion
1. If your school uses the Standard System:

Think of the mirror as the center of a math graph. Left is negative, Right is positive. Up is positive, Down is negative. Real images are always on the left and upside down → v is negative, m is negative. Virtual images are always on the right and upright → v is positive, m is positive.
2. If your school uses the Real-is-Positive System:

Forget about the graph completely. Just ask: "Is this real or virtual?" Real images can be caught on a sheet of paper → v is positive, m is positive. Virtual images only look like they are inside the mirror → v is negative, m is negative.
Solved Numerical: Question 1

Problem: The radius of curvature of a convex mirror is 20 cm and it forms the image of an object kept on its principal axis, at a distance of 5 cm from the pole of the mirror. Find the distance of the object from the pole.
Solution:
Convex mirror radius of curvature (R) = +20 cm
Focal length (f) = R/2 = +20/2 = +10 cm
Convex mirrors always form virtual images behind the mirror, so image distance (v) = +5 cm
Answer: The object is at a distance of 10 cm from the pole.
